followUps: A DBMS gives you transactions, constraints and indexed queries; a folder of CSV files gives you none of these. 1. Atomic transactions with crash recovery: a transfer either fully happens or not at all, while a CSV half-written at a power cut stays corrupt. 2. Concurrency control: two users updating at once do not overwrite each other. 3. Integrity rules (types, UNIQUE, foreign keys) plus fast indexed search instead of scanning every file. Security with per-user permissions is a fourth.

Yes, SQLite is a real, fully ACID relational database; it just runs inside your application instead of as a separate server. It is great for mobile apps, desktop tools, tests and small sites. Avoid it when many machines must write to one database over a network, when you need high write concurrency (it allows one writer at a time), or when you need fine-grained user permissions and server features such as replication.

code.title: Flat files vs a DBMS: duplicates, fixes and constraints

followUps: Data independence means you can change how data is stored or arranged without rewriting the programs that use it. Physical independence: adding an index or moving a table to another disk changes speed only, queries stay the same. Logical independence: adding a column or splitting a table behind a view does not break existing queries. Example: SELECT name FROM users keeps working after you add a phone column.

An update anomaly happens when the same fact is stored in many rows and you change only some of them. Example: a sheet lists orders with the customer's city on each row. Asha moves from Pune to Mumbai; you fix 2 of her 3 rows. Now the data says she lives in two cities and no one knows which is right. Storing the city once in a customers table, linked by id, removes the problem.

code.title: Finding super, candidate and primary keys by brute force
code.python:
import sqlite3
from itertools import combinations

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.executescript("""
CREATE TABLE students(student_id INT, roll_no INT, email TEXT, name TEXT);
INSERT INTO students VALUES (1,101,'a@x.com','Ann'),(2,102,'b@x.com','Ann'),(3,103,'c@x.com','Raj');
""")
cols = ["student_id", "roll_no", "email", "name"]
supers = []
for n in range(1, len(cols) + 1):
    for combo in combinations(cols, n):
        c = ", ".join(combo)
        total = db.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM students").fetchone()[0]
        distinct = db.execute(f"SELECT COUNT(*) FROM (SELECT DISTINCT {c} FROM students)").fetchone()[0]
        if total == distinct:  # unique on this data -> super key
            supers.append(set(combo))
print("super keys:", len(supers))
# candidate key = super key with no smaller super key inside it
cands = [s for s in supers if not any(o < s for o in supers)]
print("candidate keys:", [sorted(c) for c in cands])
print("primary key choice: student_id; alternates: roll_no, email")

followUps: It has 8 super keys. A super key is any column set containing a candidate key, and with only {A} as candidate key every super key must contain A. For each of the other columns B, C, D you freely choose in or out, so 2^3 = 8 sets: {A}, {A,B}, {A,C}, {A,D}, {A,B,C}, {A,B,D}, {A,C,D}, {A,B,C,D}.

In a true relation, no: a relation is a set of distinct rows, so the set of all columns is always a super key, and some minimal subset of it is a candidate key. In SQL, however, a table with no constraints can hold fully identical duplicate rows, so it may have no key at all. That is bad design, because you cannot update or delete one specific row; add a primary key.

code.title: Surrogate key keeps links stable when the natural key changes

followUps: Auto-increment is best for B+tree inserts, UUIDv4 worst, UUIDv7 close to auto-increment. Auto-increment and UUIDv7 grow over time, so new keys go to the right-most leaf page: pages fill fully and stay in cache. Random UUIDv4 lands anywhere in the tree, causing page splits, half-empty pages and cache misses; at millions of rows inserts slow down noticeably. UUIDv7 starts with a timestamp, so it is ordered like an increment but still unguessable and generatable anywhere.

Duplicate real users appear: two rows with the same email can now exist because the surrogate id is always different. Login by email becomes ambiguous, and emails or reports double count. Example: ids 1 and 2 both hold a@x.com. The fix is ALTER TABLE users ADD CONSTRAINT uq_email UNIQUE (email), after first cleaning the existing duplicates.

code.title: Foreign keys reject orphans and protect parents

followUps: Both refuse a change that would orphan children; the difference is timing. RESTRICT checks immediately, before anything else runs. NO ACTION checks at the end of the statement (and, if the constraint is deferrable, can wait until commit), so a trigger or later step may repair the data first. In MySQL and SQLite they behave almost the same, in PostgreSQL the deferrable behaviour of NO ACTION is the real difference.

Because the database must find children quickly whenever a parent is deleted or re-keyed, and joins use the column too. Without an index it scans the whole child table. Example: deleting 1 customer from a 10 million row orders table without an index on orders.customer_id means 10 million row checks (and long locks); with an index it is a few page reads. PostgreSQL does not create this index for you.

code.title: CASCADE helps for line items and hurts for history

followUps:
Keep the order rows and erase or anonymise only the personal data. Replace name, email and address on the user and order records with placeholders ('deleted') or null them, keep order id, amounts, dates and tax lines for the 7 years, then hard delete later. Use ON DELETE RESTRICT or SET NULL on the order's user id, not CASCADE.

UPDATE users SET name='deleted', email=NULL WHERE id=7;
UPDATE orders SET ship_name='deleted' WHERE user_id=7;

The foreign key column must allow NULL, so it must not be declared NOT NULL. When the parent is deleted, the database sets the child's FK to NULL instead of failing or deleting. Example: orders.salesperson_id INT NULL REFERENCES staff(id) ON DELETE SET NULL: when a salesperson leaves, their orders stay but show no salesperson. Declaring NOT NULL plus SET NULL makes the delete fail.

code.title: 1:N, 1:1 and N:M tables with constraints

followUps: Because one cell then holds several values, which breaks the rule that each column stores one atomic value. You cannot join, index or enforce a foreign key on it. Checking whether a student takes course 10 in '10,11,12' needs string matching that wrongly also hits '110'. Removing a course means rewriting the whole string. A junction table row per pair solves all of these with real constraints.

Use a table with a three-column key: supplies(supplier_id, part_id, project_id, qty, PRIMARY KEY (supplier_id, part_id, project_id)), with three foreign keys. One row means that supplier supplies that part to that project. Do not replace it with three pairwise tables, because that cannot record which supplier sent which part to which project (the combination is the fact).

code.title: Junction table as two 1:N links, and the retake problem

followUps: It stops being a valid key when the same pair can legitimately occur twice. A student who fails a course and retakes it next semester needs two rows for (student 1, course 10), but the pair key rejects the second. Add the semester so the key becomes (student_id, course_id, semester): row (1,10,'2025F') and row (1,10,'2026S') then coexist. Run the program to see the rejection.

Composite PK is usually right when the table only links two things and nothing else points at a row: it is smaller, uses one index and blocks duplicates automatically. Use a surrogate id plus UNIQUE (student_id, course_id) when other tables reference the junction rows, when the ORM needs a single id, or when the pair may repeat (then UNIQUE includes the semester). Either way, add an index for the reverse direction.

code.title: Classifying SQL statements into DDL, DML, DQL, DCL, TCL
code.python:
import sqlite3

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
CATEGORY = {"CREATE": "DDL", "ALTER": "DDL", "DROP": "DDL", "TRUNCATE": "DDL",
            "INSERT": "DML", "UPDATE": "DML", "DELETE": "DML",
            "SELECT": "DQL", "GRANT": "DCL", "REVOKE": "DCL",
            "BEGIN": "TCL", "COMMIT": "TCL", "ROLLBACK": "TCL", "SAVEPOINT": "TCL"}
statements = [
    "CREATE TABLE t(id INT, v TEXT)", "INSERT INTO t VALUES (1,'a')",
    "UPDATE t SET v='b'", "SELECT * FROM t", "BEGIN", "DELETE FROM t",
    "ROLLBACK", "ALTER TABLE t ADD COLUMN w INT", "GRANT SELECT ON t TO analyst",
    "TRUNCATE TABLE t", "DROP TABLE t"]
db.isolation_level = None  # we send BEGIN/ROLLBACK ourselves
NOT_IN_SQLITE = {"GRANT", "TRUNCATE"}
for s in statements:
    word = s.split()[0]
    note = "(skipped: not in SQLite)" if word in NOT_IN_SQLITE else ""
    if not note:
        db.execute(s)
    print(f"{CATEGORY[word]}  {s}  {note}")
# permission idea: an analyst role only gets DQL
allowed = {"DQL"}
print("analyst may run:", [s for s in statements if CATEGORY[s.split()[0]] in allowed])

followUps: TRUNCATE is classed as DDL, because it deallocates the table's storage (it works on the table, not on single rows), it cannot use WHERE, and in some systems it commits automatically. It looks like DELETE without WHERE, which is DML. Note that behaviour varies: in MySQL and Oracle it commits implicitly, in PostgreSQL and SQL Server it can be rolled back.

An AI agent should get only DQL (SELECT), on a read-only account limited to the tables it needs. Allow limited DML (INSERT/UPDATE) only for named tables and with human review for anything that changes money or personal data. Never give DDL, DCL or TCL: DROP or GRANT by mistake is irreversible and expands access. Enforce this with database roles and permissions, not by trusting the prompt.

code.title: DELETE vs DROP: rows, counters and the table itself
code.python:
import sqlite3

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.executescript("""
CREATE TABLE t(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT, v TEXT);
INSERT INTO t(v) VALUES ('a'),('b'),('c'),('d');
""")
count = lambda: db.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM t").fetchone()[0]
print("start rows:", count())
db.execute("DELETE FROM t WHERE v IN ('a','b')")        # DELETE with WHERE: some rows
print("after DELETE WHERE:", count())
db.execute("DELETE FROM t")                              # all rows, table remains
print("after DELETE all:", count(), "| counter kept:",
      db.execute("SELECT seq FROM sqlite_sequence WHERE name='t'").fetchone()[0])
db.execute("INSERT INTO t(v) VALUES ('e')")
print("next id keeps counting:", db.execute("SELECT id FROM t").fetchone()[0])
db.execute("DROP TABLE t")                               # table definition gone
try:
    db.execute("SELECT * FROM t")
except sqlite3.OperationalError as e:
    print("after DROP:", e)

followUps: TRUNCATE is usually refused when a foreign key points at the table, even if the child table is empty. It removes pages without checking each row against the references, so the database cannot prove no child rows depend on it. PostgreSQL needs TRUNCATE parent CASCADE (which also empties the children) or dropping the FK first; SQL Server requires dropping the constraint. DELETE checks per row and works.

Use TRUNCATE for a nightly staging reload, since a staging table has no incoming foreign keys and no WHERE is needed. It is much faster than DELETE for millions of rows because it does not log each row, and it resets identity counters. Example: TRUNCATE TABLE stg_orders; then bulk load. Use DELETE if a trigger must fire or if you must be sure it rolls back in MySQL; never DROP, as the table is needed tomorrow.

code.title: COMMIT, ROLLBACK and SAVEPOINT in a transfer
code.python:
import sqlite3

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:", isolation_level=None)  # manual BEGIN/COMMIT
db.executescript("CREATE TABLE acct(name TEXT PRIMARY KEY, bal INT CHECK(bal >= 0));"
                 "INSERT INTO acct VALUES ('A',100),('B',50);")
show = lambda tag: print(tag, db.execute("SELECT * FROM acct ORDER BY name").fetchall())

db.execute("BEGIN")
db.execute("UPDATE acct SET bal=bal-30 WHERE name='A'")
db.execute("UPDATE acct SET bal=bal+30 WHERE name='B'")
db.execute("COMMIT")
show("after committed transfer:")

db.execute("BEGIN")
db.execute("UPDATE acct SET bal=bal-20 WHERE name='A'")
db.execute("SAVEPOINT sp")                       # a point we can return to
db.execute("UPDATE acct SET bal=bal+999 WHERE name='B'")
db.execute("ROLLBACK TO sp")                     # undo only the work after sp
db.execute("COMMIT")
show("after savepoint rollback:")

db.execute("BEGIN")
try:
    db.execute("UPDATE acct SET bal=bal-500 WHERE name='A'")  # breaks CHECK
except sqlite3.IntegrityError:
    db.execute("ROLLBACK")
    print("failed update -> ROLLBACK")
show("final:")

followUps: Each autocommit statement is its own transaction, so each of the 100k inserts waits for a durable log write (fsync) to disk. At about 1 ms per flush that is around 100 seconds. Wrapping them in one BEGIN ... COMMIT pays for one flush at the end, often making the load 10 to 100 times faster. Batches of a few thousand rows are a good balance, so a failure does not lose everything.

The database detects the closed connection and rolls the transaction back, so none of its changes become permanent. Locks it held are released then. There can be a delay (the server may only notice after a timeout), during which other sessions wait on its locks. Example: after the debit but before the credit, a crash leaves both accounts unchanged, which is exactly atomicity.

code.title: NULL pitfalls: =, NOT IN, UNIQUE and aggregates
code.python:
import sqlite3

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.executescript("""
CREATE TABLE a(x INT); INSERT INTO a VALUES (1),(2),(3);
CREATE TABLE b(y INT); INSERT INTO b VALUES (1),(NULL);
CREATE TABLE u(email TEXT UNIQUE); INSERT INTO u VALUES (NULL),(NULL),('p@x.com');
CREATE TABLE s(v INT); INSERT INTO s VALUES (10),(20),(NULL);
""")
q = lambda sql: db.execute(sql).fetchall()
print("x = NULL          :", q("SELECT x FROM a WHERE x = NULL"))
print("1 = NULL gives    :", q("SELECT 1 = NULL"))
print("NOT IN with NULL  :", q("SELECT x FROM a WHERE x NOT IN (SELECT y FROM b)"))
print("NOT IN w/o NULL   :", q("SELECT x FROM a WHERE x NOT IN (SELECT y FROM b WHERE y IS NOT NULL)"))
print("UNIQUE many NULLs :", q("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM u"))
print("COUNT(*), COUNT(v), AVG(v):", q("SELECT COUNT(*), COUNT(v), AVG(v) FROM s"))
print("IS NULL           :", q("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM s WHERE v IS NULL"))

followUps: Because NOT IN means x <> v1 AND x <> v2 AND ..., and a comparison with NULL is UNKNOWN, not true. For x=2 and list (1, NULL): 2<>1 is true, 2<>NULL is unknown, and true AND unknown is unknown, so the row is dropped. Use NOT EXISTS or add WHERE y IS NOT NULL in the subquery.

COUNT(*) counts rows, COUNT(col) counts only rows where col is not NULL. Example: values 10, 20, NULL give COUNT(*)=3 but COUNT(v)=2, and AVG(v)=15 because the NULL is skipped, not treated as zero. COUNT(DISTINCT col) counts unique non-null values.

code.title: Photo, tag and follow schema with constraints

followUps: Keep the follower count as a stored counter on users (or in a separate stats table) and update it in the same transaction as each follow or unfollow. Counting rows in follows with COUNT(*) at 100M users is too slow for every profile view. Example: UPDATE users SET followers = followers + 1 WHERE user_id = 7. For very popular accounts, split the counter into several rows or use a cache and refresh it periodically, and reconcile with a nightly COUNT.

Photos: yes, a photo has no meaning without its owner, so CASCADE is reasonable (or use soft delete first). Follows: yes, rows where the user is follower or followee are meaningless afterwards, so cascade both columns. Be careful: deleting a user with millions of followers is a huge delete, so run it in batches. If you must keep history or comply with retention, use RESTRICT plus soft delete.

code.title: Expand, backfill, contract migration for NOT NULL
code.python:
import sqlite3

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:", isolation_level=None)
db.execute("CREATE TABLE users(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT)")
db.executemany("INSERT INTO users(name) VALUES (?)", [(f"user{i}",) for i in range(1, 6)])
# 1 expand: add a nullable column (cheap)
db.execute("ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN country TEXT")
# 2 backfill in small batches so locks stay short
while True:
    cur = db.execute("""UPDATE users SET country='IN' WHERE id IN
        (SELECT id FROM users WHERE country IS NULL LIMIT 2)""")
    print("batch updated", cur.rowcount, "rows")
    if cur.rowcount == 0:
        break
# 3 contract: SQLite cannot add NOT NULL later, so rebuild the table in a transaction
db.execute("BEGIN")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE users_new(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, country TEXT NOT NULL)")
db.execute("INSERT INTO users_new SELECT id, name, country FROM users")
db.execute("DROP TABLE users")
db.execute("ALTER TABLE users_new RENAME TO users")
db.execute("COMMIT")
print("rows:", db.execute("SELECT * FROM users").fetchall())
try:
    db.execute("INSERT INTO users(name) VALUES ('x')")
except sqlite3.IntegrityError as e:
    print("constraint now active:", e)

followUps: SQLite cannot change a column's constraint in place, so you rebuild the table inside a transaction. Steps: 1 turn foreign keys off, 2 BEGIN, 3 create new_t with the new definition, 4 copy rows, 5 drop the old table, 6 rename new_t, 7 recreate indexes, triggers and views, 8 check with PRAGMA foreign_key_check, 9 COMMIT, 10 turn foreign keys on. FKs go off first because DROP TABLE would otherwise delete or cascade through child rows.

Make each migration small, so there is little to undo, and write a reverse (down) migration as another step, since MySQL commits DDL immediately and cannot roll it back. Example: if step 2 of 3 fails, run the compensating statement ALTER TABLE t DROP COLUMN c. Use tools that record applied versions, test on a copy first, take a backup, and prefer online schema change tools (gh-ost, pt-osc) that keep the original table until a final swap.

code.title: Transactional outbox between two service databases
code.python:
import sqlite3, json

users = sqlite3.connect(":memory:", isolation_level=None)   # users service database
orders = sqlite3.connect(":memory:", isolation_level=None)  # orders service database
users.executescript("CREATE TABLE users(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT);"
    "CREATE TABLE outbox(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, event TEXT, sent INT DEFAULT 0);"
    "INSERT INTO users VALUES (1,'Ann'),(2,'Raj');")
orders.executescript("CREATE TABLE orders(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, user_id INT, ship_name TEXT);"
    "INSERT INTO orders VALUES (100,1,'Ann'),(101,1,'Ann'),(102,2,'Raj');")

# the delete and the event commit together (the outbox idea)
users.execute("BEGIN")
users.execute("DELETE FROM users WHERE id=1")
users.execute("INSERT INTO outbox(event) VALUES (?)", (json.dumps({"type": "UserDeleted", "user_id": 1}),))
users.execute("COMMIT")

# a relay reads unsent events and delivers them (at-least-once)
for oid, ev in users.execute("SELECT id, event FROM outbox WHERE sent=0").fetchall():
    e = json.loads(ev)
    if e["type"] == "UserDeleted":  # orders service reacts: anonymise, keep history
        orders.execute("UPDATE orders SET ship_name='ANONYMISED' WHERE user_id=?", (e["user_id"],))
    users.execute("UPDATE outbox SET sent=1 WHERE id=?", (oid,))
print("orders:", orders.execute("SELECT * FROM orders").fetchall())
print("outbox:", users.execute("SELECT * FROM outbox").fetchall())

followUps: The outbox pattern writes the event into an outbox table in the same local transaction as the business change, so either both happen or neither does. A separate relay process then reads unsent rows and publishes them to the message broker, marking them sent. It avoids the dual write problem (database updated but message lost). Delivery is at-least-once, so consumers must be idempotent.

Merge them when the services are always changed together, when you need real foreign keys and multi-table transactions across them, or when the event plumbing and reconciliation cost more than the independence is worth. Example: a small team running users and orders that deploy together and constantly hit consistency bugs. A modular monolith with one database is simpler and gives referential integrity for free.
